There are approximately 40-45 million digital nomads worldwide, according to a 2026 report

According to an estimate based on the Nomads.com report "The 2026 State of Digital Nomads," there will be around 40-45 million digital nomads globally by 2026, and this number continues to grow. The typical representative of this group, based on user data from the platform, is a male aged 30-40 from North America or Europe, with an annual income ranging from $50,000 to $250,000.

The data comes from a report built on information about Nomads.com users. It indicates that the average digital nomad most often holds a bachelor's degree, works full-time or runs a startup, and does not identify as religious. The average age in the sample is about 37 years.

The report notes that a significant portion of the community consists of established professionals and entrepreneurs with relatively high incomes, rather than just young backpackers. At the same time, the ability to live and work from anywhere in the world is still not equally accessible to everyone. Popular cities among users include Bangkok, London, Barcelona, Paris, and New York.

📌 Governance Snapshots: Why Your Tokens May Not Count in a DAO Vote

Main Points
⏺ Some DAOs calculate voting power using token balances from a specific blockchain block
⏺ Buying tokens after that snapshot may not increase your voting power
⏺ This post explains how balance snapshots work and why purchase timing matters

1️⃣ Core Idea — the protocol records balances at a selected block to determine how many votes each participant receives.
2️⃣ Why It Exists — a fixed reference point prevents voting power from changing every time tokens are transferred during the voting process.
3️⃣ Example — a vote uses balances from block #1000, but you buy tokens at block #1005. Those new tokens won't increase your voting power for that proposal.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — users may buy governance tokens specifically to participate, only to discover the snapshot already happened.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — before buying governance tokens, check the snapshot block, delegation conditions, and voting eligibility rules.

Final Thoughts

DAO governance isn't only about how many tokens you hold. It can also depend on when you held them. Sometimes your voting power is decided before the vote even begins.

Democrats Face a Defining Test: Fight Trump or Make a Deal With Him? 🏛⚖️


After scoring a decisive victory in the midterm elections and securing control of both chambers of Congress, Democrats are preparing for a new political battle in Washington. But their biggest challenge may not be defeating Trump at the ballot box. 

It will be deciding how to deal with a president who still has two years left in the White House. Beginning in January, Democrats will have the power to launch congressional investigations into Trump, his administration, members of his family and business associates. Party lawmakers have already signaled that they intend to use their new oversight authority to examine allegations of corruption, conflicts of interest and the president's use of executive power.

Yet an aggressive campaign against Trump could come with political risks. Democratic leaders know that voters who helped deliver their electoral victory will expect tangible improvements in their everyday lives, not simply another two years of political warfare. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries has promised a change in direction, arguing that Americans voted for a Congress prepared to address their economic concerns. 

Democrats have pledged to tackle rising living costs, restore healthcare funding and food assistance, reconsider Trump's sweeping tariffs and challenge his handling of the war in Iran. The problem is that many of these ambitions will require cooperation from the very president they intend to investigate. 

Trump retains the power to veto legislation, making bipartisan negotiations essential if Democrats want to turn campaign promises into actual policy. This creates a potentially difficult divide within the party. Progressive Democrats are demanding a tougher approach, including investigations and legislation designed to challenge Trump's policies directly. 

Some want action on the minimum wage, restrictions on corporate political spending, higher taxes on billionaires and tighter rules governing congressional stock trading. 

More moderate lawmakers, however, are warning against spending valuable political capital on proposals that have little chance of becoming law. They argue that Democrats should concentrate on areas where compromises are possible, particularly housing costs, healthcare access, food assistance and energy prices.

Trump himself has struck a somewhat conciliatory tone following the Republican losses, indicating that he could be willing to work with the new Democratic majority. He has said he does not want to spend the remainder of his presidency simply vetoing legislation. That does not mean the confrontation is over. 

Democratic investigations could also revive discussions about impeachment, although party leaders recognize that removing Trump from office would face significant political and constitutional obstacles. For Democrats, the stakes extend beyond the immediate struggle with the White House. 

Their performance over the next two years could determine whether voters continue to trust them with congressional power or view their victory as a temporary protest against Trump. The party now faces a difficult balancing act: holding the president accountable while demonstrating that it can govern, negotiate and deliver results. 

The question is whether Democrats can do both without allowing their internal divisions to undermine the opportunity created by their electoral victory.
